column2: In ancient Hellas, before the Event, the Eleusinian Mysteries were held, mysterious rites held in the city of Eleusis in honor of the harvest goddess Demeter, her daughter Persephone, and according to some sources also the wine god Dionysus. These mysteries were held in great esteem and were shrouded in mystery—as remains to this day. Today, Neoplatonists and Neohellenics (in the semi-Christianized version) continue to celebrate these mysteries, although the requirement that they take place in Eleusis is no longer as strictly observed.

Philosophy is the greatest science, as one of Plato's students once said. Therefore, it falls to you, a Neoplatonist like you, to explore it to the fullest extent of your ability by reading the writings of Plato and his later followers and students.

Neoplatonists, in addition to following philosophy, also follow gods—they worship many deities, which they treat more or less metaphorically, depending on their philosophical background. As one of them, you can choose or change the deity you follow.

Long ago, a powerful state existed in Greece and Anatolia, the Eastern Roman Empire—the Byzantine Empire—ruled by powerful emperors, successors to Rome in the East. In 1453, the last Emperor, Constantine XII, died defending New Rome from the onslaught of Turkish invaders. Today, if you possess even the foundations of the former Eastern Roman Empire, you can restore it and become its monarch.
Many gods are worshiped by Plato's disciples. Since you are also his disciple, you can also choose a deity to be your patron.

The Eleusinian Mysteries are a major religious event formerly held in Eleusis, near Athens. They are held in honor of the goddess Demeter and her daughter Persephone, and the god Dionysus. As the organizer of this year's Mysteries, you order preparations for them.

Today begins the Eleusinian Mysteries – the priests announce this in the morning before the temples. The entire population soon gathers in one city, and chants in honor of Demeter begin. One young man, chosen by the priests from among the people, recites a traditional song in honor of Demeter, praising her for the fertile soil of Hellas. Then the people, and you with them, march to the nearest waters with a suckling pig for sacrifice. There, everyone bathes in water, and the priests clean the suckling pig, simultaneously singing of their desire to offer the best sacrifice to the goddess of fertility. Afterward, you return to the city, where the priest sacrifices the suckling pig on the altar, praying to Demeter for a bountiful harvest. Afterward, you return to your room, knowing that this is only the beginning of the mysteries.

Fasting begins on the second day of the Mysteries. By order of the priests, all meat that cannot be preserved during the fast is ritually burned in the marketplace in honor of Demeter. You spend the entire day in the temple, singing hymns to Demeter and Persephone, and watching theater performances depicting various myths, not just those related to the goddess worshiped in the Mysteries. After a full day of fasting, you return hungry and enjoy a simple meal before bed.
It's dark, Demeter won't see me eating more....

The second and final day of fasting begins. Animal and material sacrifices are still being made in the marketplace and temples, and in the streets, choirs sing songs to women about Demeter and Persephone. You, on the other hand, continue to fast, although the next day the priests no longer frown upon eating two modest meals before evening. The day ends with the announcement of the fourth day, when the fast ends, and festivities and a grand feast begin in the marketplace, during which tables are said to be groaning with food. According to some priests, it's a good omen if one of the tables fails to support the weight of the food and is destroyed.

The fourth day of the mysteries begins – large tables are set in the market square, and you, as ruler of this land, take your place of honor around the priests. The people rejoice and feast with such vigor that servants quickly have to bring more food and drink to keep the table from emptying. A chorus of women, considered a gathering of the best local singers, sings a solemn song of joy about the meeting of Demeter and Persephone. Soon, the feast has dragged on for several hours. You return home, stuffed, feeling that eating anything more would make you vomit – a stark contrast to the previous two days.

In the morning, the priests announce a grand procession to the local sanctuary. Many people gather for the procession, and you, as ruler of these lands, lead the procession, followed closely by the priests. During the pilgrimage, many sing joyful hymns to Demeter and Persephone, giving thanks for last year's harvest and praying for a good harvest this summer. After some time, you leave the city and arrive at the sanctuary walls. There, you pitch your tents, and the priests offer offerings on the temple steps. According to custom, tomorrow will be the culmination of the mysteries. During this time, the procession members sleep in tents in front of the sanctuary, while the priests pray inside, preparing the sanctuary for the next day.

In the morning, the priests awaken the people camping outside the temple, including you. They joyfully announce the news, sad for many, that this is the last day of the mystery. The priests begin to sing a song of thanksgiving about a mother's love and the joy of having their lost daughter back. The people camping outside the sanctuary gather their tents and follow you inside. After a while, you gather inside
column3: the hall miraculously accommodates you. Actors hired by the priests perform a play about Hades' abduction of Persephone, Demeter's search for her, the mother's determination of her daughter's fate, and the daughter's reunion after winter. After the play, the actors receive a fee from you and the priests, after which the priests hand out cups filled with a strange-looking and smelling liquid and order you to drink it.

column2: You refuse to drink the liquid offered to you and ostentatiously pour it out. This causes shock on the faces of everyone gathered. The priests are outraged and ask, "You're telling me you don't intend to look at the gods after drinking this liquid," claiming that why would the gods make their arrival contingent on drinking something? The indignant priest orders you to leave, which you do, leaving the shocked people behind.

You pretend to drink it, but the liquid ends up somewhere other than your body. After a moment, you see other people begin to howl in ecstasy and shout something incomprehensible. You stare at it, bewildered. The priests are shouting praises to the divine Demeter and her daughter. The man next to you is in a state of extreme euphoria, shouting that he sees his daughter next to Demeter. You are shocked by it all. After a while, when the people emerge from their ecstasy, the priest recites the ritual formula and makes the final animal sacrifice. You leave the sanctuary in a state of severe shock.

You drink the liquid. After a moment, you feel your body lose its temperature. Everything begins to take on vibrant colors, and time seems to stand still. You hear a voice and a great light blinds you. After a moment, you see her – Demeter, dressed in diamond robes and a golden crown, and on her right, Persephone, dressed in an equally beautiful gown, and on your left, Dionysus with his satyrs, singing songs of wine and feasts. You see many people around them, mostly the dead, who perished years ago in plagues or wars. You feel euphoria, you scream, calling out to familiar faces in the distance. After a moment, it all disappears, and you feel as if it's all over. The priest recites the final prayers, sacrifices an animal, and the people, along with you, leave the sanctuary, ending this year's mysteries.

This is great news for the entire world, for what was never meant to return has returned.

Years ago, Prince Lazar Sratsimir, known by usurpers as Dimitar Danielsin, the alleged son of an unprincipled, bankrupt merchant from Silven, set out to claim his throne, ending his reign de jure on the gallows in Sofia. Now, as his descendant and rightful heir, you, as the King of Bulgaria, can clear his name and officially become a member and head of the Sratsimir family.
Today you issued an official proclamation, Prince Lazar Sratsimir survived and was not killed by his sister Anna as the official propaganda and the voice of chroniclers have said so far.

Many years ago, the Neo-Hellenic peoples arose from the myth of Agios Odysseus, who, after defeating the Emperor's enemies in the form of the sinister Sultanate of Rum, embarked on the Odyssey. There, he spent many years in various regions of the Mediterranean, atonement for his sins by experiencing, at God's will, many quarrels. Returning after 10 years, he blessed his wife, Agios Penelope, for her fidelity to their marriage vows. As a Neo-Hellenic, you can continue this tradition and embark on your own Odyssey.

Among Christians, there are pilgrimages, among Neo-Hellenics, Odysseys. An Odyssey differs from a Pilgrimage not only in its nature but also in its purpose. The goal of a pilgrimage is penance, the goal of an Odyssey is glory and the acquisition of experience, while the religious goal is secondary. Today, you are faced with planning an Odyssey, your journey to a goal during which you will overcome successive adversities.
Within the Greek world I will wander
Give up on going to the Odyssey

Outside the Greek world, Neohellenics are dangerous. Neohellenics originate in Greece and are not a native faith of the much larger Italy or traditionally Muslim-Christian Egypt. These places, though important for their heritage of the unified Mediterranean and for carrying the Christos-Dias Sun far to the East, are less frequently visited by Neohellenics than Greek cities.

The Greek world is well known to Neo-Hellenics, who have always praised it as the homeland of all wisdom, philosophy, and courage. It was here that Christos-Dias clashed with the ancient, old gods, and here too, many saints were born, bringing light to the four corners of the world. Neo-Hellenics have three holy places here: Athens, where freedom was born, Constantinople, where strength was born, and the Monastery of Mount Athos, where pontificate and monastic practices were born. Choose your destination wisely.
Preparations completed, prayers offered by the priests for the success of your Odyssey, it is time to set off on your journey.

You reach Athens, the capital of Hellas. This is where Pericles was born, where they said no to the Persians, and where the tyrant Nero stopped years ago. You reflect on how the republic flourished here before the Event, how people feared God and his saints. You observe temples old and new from afar. Soon you ascend, passing shepherds and old people, until you reach the summit of the Acropolis. There you see many statues and inscriptions, ancient inscriptions praising the intercession of Saint Demeter, a statue of Saint Poseidon, and many other remnants of the ancient Empire. You pause here, and like the Athenians of 2,000 years ago, you gaze and observe their city.

You arrive in the peninsula of Holy Athos. In the distance, you see the ancient Monastery of the Great Lavra, founded over a millennium ago by the great saint: Athanasios. As you walk closer to the Lavra, you hear the blessed hymns recounting the tradition of the Mountain all the way back to its earliest foundations of the Theotokos’s trip with the Apostle John to visit her Son’s friend, Lazarus, on Cyprus, where she would be blown off course to the then-pagan Athos. The Blessed Virgin would walk ashore and be overwhelmed by the mountain’s wonderful and wild natural beauty. Then she blessed it and asked her Son for it to be her garden. And a voice was heard saying, “Let this place be your inheritance and your garden, a paradise and a haven of salvation for those seeking to be saved.” Like any devout pilgrim, you dwell on this blessed tradition and are brought to prayer in glorification of the Lord.

You arrive in Alexandria, the city of Alexander the Great, one of the greatest conquerors of the pre-Event era, lord of lands from Albania to Pakistan. During his time or that of his descendants, this city was built as a symbol of his glory and legacy. This city has always been a melting pot of cultures, a meeting point of pagan, Christian, and Islamic cultures. You pass through this city, and just as a thousand years ago, so today, there are crowds of people from all the surrounding lands. Passing them, you reach the Column of Pompey the Great and continue, contemplating the glory of this conqueror, until you reach the largest temple built in honor of Christ, the Cathedral of the Annunciation, also known as the Evangelismos. As you enter, you see a magnificent iconostasis. You kneel before it and offer prayers to your God and the saints.

You reach Rome, the Eternal City. It was here that Emperor after Emperor reigned, true "Exoterikoí Episkopoi," who fought the infidel Saracens, Persians, and Germans, and carried the splendor of the Mediterranean peoples throughout the world. You pass old churches, merchants, pilgrims, and locals. You walk through ancient streets that remember the days before the Event, and you reach the Roman Forum, where Roman senators long ago gathered to debate matters divine and human, life and death. You kneel and remember the glory of Old Rome, which has passed but will return.

You have finally arrived at Constantinople, now taken by foreign infidels though still filled with the memory of its ancient history. Before you rises an immense and ancient metropolis whose towering walls, crowded harbors, and countless domes dwarf every city you have seen upon your Odyssey. As you make your way through the winding streets in search of lodging, your senses are overcome by the cries of merchants, the mingling scents of incense and spice, and the endless throngs of travelers and sailors from far and wide. Along your path stand the ancient ruins of churches, monasteries, and monuments, many transformed to serve the new rulers or left to rot yet they still bear witness to the city’s long and sacred history. Like any devout traveller of your religion, you press onward through the bustling crowds with solemn wonder and anticipation, longing at last to behold the Patriarchal Cathedral of St. George and to offer prayers to God amidst the fading remnants of Second Rome’s once-glorious inheritance.
This is the end of your Odyssey. You have returned home and earned the title of successor to Saint Odysseus, a sign of true courage among your fellow believers.
The ship you are sailing on is attacked by pirates hungry for riches and your blood.

You meet a group of people who tell you they're looking for sirens and satyrs that are prowling the area. They say they haven't seen them yet, but they have a hunch and have heard they're in the area, harassing the locals.
Leave them and hope they come to their senses.
After a long search, I conclude that you found nothing and all your time was wasted.

Just when you thought you couldn't find anything, a strange animal attacked you—a goat, you thought—and you instinctively killed it, which then rolled into the sea. Your companions ran up and said you'd apparently killed a satyr that was troubling the local population, and they called you "Satyr Killer."

During your journey, you encounter other travelers embarking on their Odyssey. When you speak with them, they invite you to a friendly fistfight, touting it as a chance to improve your fighting skills.

You pass a village and see peasants gathered in the fields, all sorts of amusement and laughter, singing songs about the heroic Hector of Turkey, slain by the impetuous Achilles, son of Saint Thetis. Suddenly, someone calls to you from afar to approach them.

The villagers soon surround you like nothing, and they begin to hum the tale of Achilles and Hector. Many years ago, the Byzantine Empire was at war with the Sultanate of Rum, which had usurped the succession from the First Rome. Its leader was Sultan Priam, a reckless man, father of the equally reckless Paris, but also honorable Hector. The war lasted ten years, until the siege of Rum's capital, Troy, came. During the siege, a battle ensued and Achilles faced Prince Hector. They dueled for a long time until a demon tricked Hector and caused Achilles to kill Hector. Shortly thereafter, Paris himself killed Achilles by shooting him in the knee with a crossbow, then correcting the shot to the head. Troy ultimately fell and was destroyed, but Hector' sister, Cassandra, saw a vision in which she saw angels carrying Hector to heaven, where he kissed the cross the angels carried, and Achilles, despite fighting on the side of Christos-Dias, went to hell for his pride and lust. When the villagers finished telling their story, you knew it was interesting and worth the pause.

After hearing the story, you stopped in the village for a day. It turned out there was a wedding taking place nearby, and as a surprise guest and a change of pace for the local community, you were invited to attend. But now, you had to continue your journey.

As you travel, you come across abandoned monasteries. Entering, you greet the remaining paintings and icons, and then proceed to the monastery garden. It turns out the monastery has been empty for a very long time.
Go to the chapel and pray
Admire the beauty of the monastery and sing songs about ancient times
You arrive at a monastery filled with monks. You knock on the monastery gate and are welcomed as guests for the day.
Stay here permanently as a monk
While sailing, you come to a port. You hear about the wrestling taking place there, and at the urging of another traveler, you go there.
During your journey, you stop at a town with an theatre. You learn that Greek and Roman plays are performed there.

You're sitting comfortably in the theater after buying a ticket. There are a lot of other people around you, some with food purchased from the theater owner, others, not entirely in compliance with building regulations, have smuggled in their own, much cheaper provisions. The play you've come to see is "Clouds" by Aristophanes, an ancient writer. It tells the story of Strepsiades, a family man who has the misfortune of having a son, Pheidippides, who has a lot of creditors and an obsession with horses. To cope with the constant need to repay loans, Strepsiades goes to Socrates and his sophists to learn the science of words and how to wriggle out of his son's debts in any court. However, after several trials, Socrates decides that old men is too dump, so the father sends his son, who has better results, to the sophists. Then you see a scene of a verbal duel between the just and unjust Logos, the latter winning and taking the young man under his protection. Upon his return, the son waives all his debts, but thanks to his sophistication, he also "proves" that he has the right to beat his father, which causes the enraged father to set fire to Socrates' house.

You're sitting comfortably in the theater after buying a ticket. There are a lot of other people around you, some with food purchased from the theater owner, others, not entirely in compliance with building regulations, have smuggled in their own, much cheaper provisions. The play you've come to see is "Octavia" written centuries ago by an author whose name has vanished into the mists of time. The play tells the story of the struggle for the tyrant Nero's heart between his legitimate wife, Octavia, and his lover, Poppaea Sabina, who wants to take his place. During the play, the chorus laments Octavia's fate. The demonic Agrippina, who wasn't satisfied with disrupting the state's rule during her lifetime, appears and predicts Nero's defeat. Ultimately, Nero exiles Octavia to the island of Pandataria, where she is executed. The play ends with the chorus predicting what will happen to Nero's dynasty and that it will meet a disastrous end.

You're sitting comfortably in the theater after buying a ticket. There are a lot of other people around you, some with food purchased from the theater owner, others, not entirely in compliance with building regulations, have smuggled in their own, much cheaper provisions. The play you've come to see is "Antigone" written centuries ago by Sophocles. The play tells the story of Antigone's conflict with her uncle Creon over the body of her brother Polynices, who attempted to usurp his brother's throne and was slained. Antigone invokes divine law in her resolution, while Creon invokes his own, declaring that whoever buries the traitor will be killed. However, Antigone attempts to bury the body, is caught, and Creon pronounces her condemned to death by starvation. Creon is later persuaded by his son Haemon and his wife Eurydice to change his mind. The play ultimately ends with Antigone committing suicide, followed by Haemon discovering Antigone's death, and finally, Eurydice, who learns of Heamon's death. Finally, Creon, distraught, buries Polynices' body.
